transcript.content:
This would be amazing if I could see it. I really hope the Moon is visible right now!

I'm in Edinburgh, Scotland, UK at 2026-09-29 19:59 BST (UTC+0100) (2026-09-29T18:59:00Z in UTC), at latitude 55.9533 degrees and longitude -3.1883 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -9.415 degrees and its azimuth is 280.21 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 5.272 degrees and its azimuth is 59.687 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 88.2 percent illuminated, 139.714 degrees from the Sun, and 370221.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is nautical twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

At 5.3° altitude, the Moon is quite low in the northeast (azimuth about 60°, east-northeast), so the main issue is whether your view in that direction is blocked by buildings, hills, trees, or haze near the horizon. But if you have a reasonably open horizon, an 88%-illuminated Moon is bright enough to be easily visible to the naked eye.

Nautical twilight means the sky is still somewhat bright, but a waxing/waning gibbous Moon that high above the horizon should stand out, especially in clear conditions. Its 140° separation from the Sun also places it well away from the remaining twilight glow in the west.

Look low toward the ENE, roughly a little over one fist-width held at arm’s length above a flat horizon. Give your eyes a moment and scan slowly; atmospheric extinction and low-altitude haze can make it look yellower, dimmer, or distorted, but it should still be conspicuous if unobstructed.
